mainTopic: Taking collateral: the court agent's rights, what a debtor must be left (סידור), and whether collateral is sold
overview: This amud deals with how a debt is collected and what must be left for the borrower. First the גמרא shows that תנאים disagree about whether a שליח בית דין must wait outside like the lender or may go into the house. A ברייתא then teaches that food-making tools may not be taken, and that the borrower keeps two beds for himself. Those beds follow the rule of סידור, which is learned from ערכין. The גמרא explains that one bed is for eating and one is for sleeping, based on a health warning from שמואל. Next, רב נחמן asks how there can be סידור if collateral is sold. The גמרא explains that he was speaking according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. It proves that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל means a full sale, because he holds that all Jews are children of kings. Finally, רב חגא challenges the whole idea of leaving the borrower anything, and אביי's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The court agent is treated like the lender
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the earlier attempted proof. It says the שליח בית דין has the same rule as the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The court agent is like the lender.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the earlier attempted proof. It says the שליח בית דין follows the same rule as the מלוה: he also waits outside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier proof assumed the court agent is different from the lender. This answer removes that assumption by putting them in one group, so the proof no longer works.

keyTerms.meaning: An agent sent by the court

phrases.english: No,
the agent of the court is like the lender.
phrases.notes: In other words, he also has to stand outside and wait for the borrower to bring the collateral out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the attempted proof that came just before this section
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The earlier proof about the court agent's rule
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed the court agent is different from the lender, but he may be the same.

steps.title: A ברייתא says one פסוק is about the court agent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that reads one collateral פסוק as speaking about the lender and the other as speaking about the court agent. That suggests they have different rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'If you take your neighbor's garment as collateral' speaks about the court agent. Maybe it speaks about a lender? No. 'Do not go into his house to take his collateral' already covers the lender. So the first פסוק must be about the court agent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new proof from a ברייתא. The ברייתא says the פסוק 'אם חבל תחבל' is about a שליח בית דין, not a בעל חוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the פסוק 'לא תבא אל ביתו' is about the lender. So the other פסוק, 'אם חבל תחבל', must be about someone else: the court agent. That suggests the court agent is a separate case from the lender, and maybe he is allowed to go into the house.

keyTerms.meaning: Creditor, the one who is owed money
How then do I explain (this other פסוק)?

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"If you take your neighbor's garment as collateral"
phrases.notes: שמות 22:25

phrases.english: the verse is speaking about an agent of the court.

phrases.aramaic: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בִּשְׁלִיחַ בֵּית דִּין הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר,
phrases.english: You say the verse is speaking about an agent of the court,
or maybe it is only about a creditor?
When it says, "You shall not go into his house
phrases.notes: דברים 24:10

phrases.english: to take his collateral,"
the creditor is already covered.
So how do I explain
"If you take your neighbor's garment as collateral"?
The verse is speaking about an agent of the court!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in step 1 that the court agent is like the lender
steps.raayaObject: That a שליח בית דין has a different rule from the lender
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא splitting 'אם חבל תחבל' (court agent) from 'לא תבא אל ביתו' (lender)

steps.title: This is a מחלוקת between תנאים; first view: the agent waits outside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this is a מחלוקת between תנאים. It quotes a ברייתא that says the court agent must stand outside, just like the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a disagreement between תנאים. A ברייתא teaches: a court agent who comes to take collateral may not go into the house. He stands outside, and the borrower brings the collateral out to him, as it says, 'Stand outside, and the man…'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the proof by saying תנאים disagree about this. It quotes the first ברייתא, which holds that the court agent also must wait outside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא from step 2 holds that the court agent is different. But this ברייתא holds he is like the lender, which matches step 1. Since the question is a מחלוקת, step 1 can follow this ברייתא's view, and the proof no longer forces us one way.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a disagreement between תנאים

phrases.english: It is a disagreement between תנאים, as it is taught:
An agent of the court who comes to take collateral from him
may not go into his house to take the collateral.
Instead, he stands outside,
and the other one brings the collateral out to him,
as it says, "You shall stand outside, and the man".
phrases.notes: דברים 24:11. Notice this ברייתא quotes the words "and the man" too, while the next one stops at "stand outside."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the proof from step 2 by showing the issue is a מחלוקת between תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא proves the court agent is different from the lender
steps.terutzMaskana: Only one view holds that; another תנא says the court agent also waits outside

steps.title: Second view: only the lender waits outside; the agent may go in
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא says only the lender must stand outside. The court agent may go into the house and take the collateral.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: a lender who comes to take collateral may not go into the house. He stands outside, and the borrower goes in and brings it out to him, as it says, 'Stand outside.' But a court agent who comes to take collateral may go into the house and take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by quoting the second, opposing ברייתא. This one gives the court agent a different rule from the lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the rule 'stand outside' covers only the בעל חוב. The שליח בית דין acts for the court, so this תנא lets him go in. Together with step 3, this shows there are two clear opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: Goes in and takes the collateral

steps.whatToRemember: There are two opinions among the תנאים. One says the שליח בית דין must wait outside like the lender. The other says only the lender waits outside, and the court agent may go in.

phrases.english: And another ברייתא teaches:
A creditor who comes to take collateral from him
may not go into his house to take the collateral.
Instead, he stands outside,
and the other one goes in and brings his collateral out to him,
as it says, "You shall stand outside."
But an agent of the court who comes to take collateral from him
may go into his house and take the collateral.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer from step 3 by quoting the opposing ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone agrees on how the court agent takes collateral
steps.terutzMaskana: This תנא lets the court agent go in, which matches the ברייתא from step 2

steps.title: What must be left for the debtor
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists what may not be taken as collateral and what must be left for the debtor. It then compares this to ערכין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The agent may not take food-preparing tools as collateral. He leaves two beds and bedding for a rich man, and two beds and a mat for a poor man. These are for the debtor himself, not for his wife or children. Just as we arrange things for a debtor, so we arrange them in ערכין.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the last step keeps going. It now lists items the debtor keeps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rules are given: food-making tools are off-limits, and basic beds must be left behind. The protection covers only the debtor himself, not his family. The last line links this to ערכין, and the גמרא will question that link next.

keyTerms.meaning: they arrange (decide what a person keeps)
pledges to give a person's set value to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: And he may not take as collateral from him
items used to make food.
phrases.notes: דברים 24:6

phrases.english: And he leaves a bed, another bed, and bedding, for a rich man.
A bed, another bed, and a mat, for a poor man.
For him, but not for his wife,
and not for his sons and daughters.
Just as arrangements are made for a debtor,
so arrangements are made in ערכין.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא יְמַשְׁכְּנֶנּוּ דְּבָרִים שֶׁעוֹשִׂין בָּהֶן אוֹכֶל נֶפֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food-making tools may not be taken. Two beds plus bedding or a mat are left for the debtor alone. This is compared to ערכין.

steps.title: The comparison is backwards
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that ערכין is the Torah's main source for these arrangements, so the ברייתא has it backwards.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't that the opposite? The main source for arranging is written about ערכין!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last line of the ברייתא. It says the ברייתא compared things in the wrong direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah talks about arranging only in the section on ערכין. So ערכין should be the model, and the debtor should be learned from it. Saying ערכין is like the debtor reverses the source.

phrases.english: Isn't it the other way around?!
phrases.notes: Literally, "toward which side?" It's a way of saying the order is backwards.

phrases.english: The main source for arranging is written about ערכין!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 27:8

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of the last line of step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase comparing ערכין to a debtor
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source passage is about ערכין, so ערכין must be the model, not the thing being compared.

steps.title: Flip the wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording: debtors are arranged for the way ערכין are.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: just as arrangements are made in ערכין, so they are made for a debtor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the ברייתא by reversing the comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule itself stays the same. Only the direction changes: ערכין is the source, and a debtor is learned from it.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
Just as arrangements are made in ערכין,
so arrangements are made for a debtor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to make the debtor the source for ערכין.
steps.terutzMaskana: ערכין is the source, and the debtor's arrangement is learned from it.
steps.whatToRemember: The arrangement of what a person keeps comes from ערכין, and a debtor is treated the same way.

steps.title: Who is the second bed for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the rule about two beds and asks whom they are for.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: He leaves a bed, another bed, and bedding for a rich man, and a bed, another bed, and a mat for a poor man. For whom?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the bed rule and asks who uses the extra bed. This sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One bed seems enough for one man. So the extra bed sounds like it is meant for someone else.

phrases.english: The Master said:
He leaves a bed, another bed, and bedding for a rich man,
a bed, another bed, and a mat for a poor man.
For whom?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the bed rule from step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who the two beds are meant for.

steps.title: The beds can't be for his family
steps.stepSummary: The family can't be the answer, since the ברייתא said these items are not for his wife or children.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say they are for his wife, sons and daughters, you already said: for him, but not for his wife, sons or daughters!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the obvious answer and shows it contradicts the ברייתא itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said clearly that the protection is only for the debtor. So the second bed can't be for the family.

phrases.english: If you say: for his wife, sons and daughters,
but you said: for him,
but not for his wife, sons and daughters!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules out one possible answer to step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the extra bed is for the family
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same ברייתא excludes the wife and children.

steps.title: Both beds are for him
steps.stepSummary: Both beds belong to the debtor himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, both this one and that one are for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the debtor keeps both beds for his own use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the family is ruled out, the only option left is the debtor. This raises a new question: why does one man need two beds?

keyTerms.meaning: this one and that one, both

phrases.english: Rather, both this one and that one are for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 after step 9 ruled out the family.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both beds are for the debtor himself.

steps.title: Why does he need two?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why one person needs two beds.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need two?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that both beds are his, the גמרא asks why one bed isn't enough. This sets up the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creditor is only made to leave real needs. So a second bed for the same man needs a reason.

phrases.english: Why do I need two?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the answer in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason one debtor needs two beds.

steps.title: One to eat on, one to sleep on
steps.stepSummary: One bed is for eating and one is for sleeping, following שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: One he eats on and one he sleeps on, following שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the two beds by giving each one a different use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In those days people reclined on a bed to eat. Keeping separate beds for eating and sleeping matches a health warning of שמואל, quoted next.

phrases.english: One that he eats on
and one that he sleeps on,
following שמואל.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲדָא דְּאָכֵיל עֲלַהּ וַחֲדָא דְּזָג עֲלַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Separate beds for eating and for sleeping.

steps.title: שמואל's three dangers
steps.stepSummary: שמואל lists three harms he cannot cure. One is eating bread without walking four אמות afterward.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: I know a cure for everything except three things. Eating a bitter date on an empty stomach. Tying a wet linen belt around one's waist. Eating bread and not walking four אמות afterward.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes שמואל to back up the two-bed answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The third danger is the key one. If a man eats on one bed and sleeps on another, he has to walk a little after eating. So the second bed is a real health need.
steps.whatToRemember: A debtor keeps two beds for himself, one for eating and one for sleeping, so he walks a bit after eating, as שמואל warned.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that "basic needs" a creditor must leave include what a person needs for his health.

phrases.english: As שמואל said:
For all things, I know their cures,
except for these three:
one who eats a bitter date
on an empty stomach;
one who ties a linen belt
that is wet, around his waist;
and one who eats bread
and does not walk four אמות.
phrases.notes: This is the danger that matters here. A separate bed for sleeping makes him walk a bit after eating.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the reason in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That eating and sleeping need separate beds
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל's warning about eating bread without walking four אמות

steps.title: A ברייתא: a debtor gets arrangements like in ערכין
steps.stepSummary: A תנא recites before רב נחמן that a debtor is given 'arrangements' the same way as someone who owes ערכין.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught before רב נחמן: Just as we make arrangements in ערכין, so we make arrangements for a debtor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new section by quoting a ברייתא recited before רב נחמן. It says a debtor is left his basic needs, just like a person who owes ערכין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ערכין, when the Temple collects from someone who cannot pay, it leaves him basic necessities. This is called סידור. The ברייתא says a private creditor must do the same for a debtor.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who memorized and recited ברייתות in the בית מדרש
Make arrangements, meaning we leave the person his basic necessities
Pledges to give the Temple the fixed 'value' of a person
Here, the debtor (the one who owes money)

phrases.english: A tanna taught before Rav Naḥman:
In the way that arrangements are made for valuations,
phrases.notes: When someone owes the Temple and can't pay, it leaves him basic things like food, a bed and his work tools.

phrases.english: so arrangements are made for a debtor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion of the סידור rule from step 7, after the side discussion about the debtor's two beds.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A debtor is given סידור, his basic necessities, just as in ערכין.

steps.title: רב נחמן: if we sell it, how can we leave it to him?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן objects that collateral is sold, so it makes no sense to leave the debtor part of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Now, if we actually sell it, do we make arrangements for him?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן challenges the ברייתא. If the collateral gets sold to pay the debt, there is no room to leave the debtor his necessities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן assumes the creditor sells the collateral completely. Selling and leaving the debtor his needs pull in opposite directions, so he finds the ברייתא hard to accept.

keyTerms.meaning: We actually sell (a doubled verb for emphasis)
Now, since (used to say: if this much is true, how can the other be?)

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב נחמן answering the תנא.

phrases.english: Now, if we actually sell it,
do we make arrangements for him?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule of סידור for a debtor
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Collateral is sold, and a sale doesn't fit with leaving the debtor part of it.

steps.title: But the משנה says collateral is returned, not sold
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions רב נחמן's assumption that collateral is sold, since the משנה says it is returned when needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But do we sell it? Didn't we learn: He returns the pillow at night and the plow by day!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions רב נחמן himself. Where does he get the idea that collateral is sold? The משנה says the creditor keeps giving it back to the debtor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the משנה, the creditor returns the pillow each night and the plow each day. That means the collateral stays with the creditor and is lent back to the debtor, not sold. So רב נחמן's starting point seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it really so? (a word that opens a challenge)

phrases.english: But do we sell it?
But didn't we learn in the mishna:
He returns the pillow at night,
and the plow by day!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the assumption behind רב נחמן's objection in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's assumption that collateral is sold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה requires returning the items each day or night, which shows they are not sold.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who allows a sale
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא was taught according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who says that after thirty days the collateral is sold in court. רב נחמן's question was based on that view.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא taught it before him according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. This is what רב נחמן meant: Now, according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, we actually sell it. Do we make arrangements for him? As we learned: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says, even to the debtor himself he returns it only until thirty days. From then on he sells them in court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the ברייתא follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. רב נחמן's question means: according to him the collateral is sold, so how can there be arrangements?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that the daily returning lasts only thirty days, and after that בית דין sells the items. So the 'selling' רב נחמן talked about comes from his opinion. That makes רב נחמן's objection make sense again.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what he was saying to him (explains what someone really meant)

phrases.aramaic: תַּנָּא כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל תַּנָּא קַמֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: The tanna taught it before him according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
and this is what he was saying to him:
Now, according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
we actually sell it,
so do we make arrangements for him?

phrases.aramaic: דִּתְנַן, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As we learned: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Even to the debtor himself he does not return it
phrases.notes: The משנה just said the collateral isn't returned to the debtor's heirs. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds that even the debtor gets it back only for a while.

phrases.english: except until thirty days,
and from then on he sells them in court.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּא כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל תַּנָּא קַמֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by assigning the ברייתא and רב נחמן's question to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns the source to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן assumed a sale with no basis, against the משנה's rule of returning the items.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב נחמן was speaking according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who allows a sale after thirty days.

steps.title: Maybe רבן שמעון בן גמליאל means only a partial sale
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know רבן שמעון בן גמליאל means a full sale. Maybe after thirty days we sell only what the debtor doesn't need and return the rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know that when רבן שמעון בן גמליאל said 'sell,' he meant completely? Perhaps he means: until thirty days, the creditor returns it as is. After that, he returns what is fitting for the debtor, and we sell what is not fitting for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer by suggesting another way to read רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. Maybe his 'sale' is only partial, which would still leave room for arrangements.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If after thirty days we sell only items too fancy for the debtor and give him plain ones, that is exactly a סידור. Then רבן שמעון בן גמליאל would not contradict the ברייתא at all, and רב נחמן's objection falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do we know?

phrases.aramaic: וּמִמַּאי דְּכִי קָאָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל זַבּוֹנֵי
phrases.english: And from where do we know that when Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said "sell,"
he was saying completely?
Perhaps this is what he is saying:
Until thirty days he returns it to him as is,
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is part of the corrected wording.

phrases.aramaic: מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ מַיהְדַּר לֵיהּ לְמַאי דַּחֲזֵי לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: and from then on he returns to him what is fitting for him,
phrases.notes: He means items suited to the debtor's simple needs, rather than fancy ones.

phrases.english: and we sell what is not fitting for him?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִמַּאי דְּכִי קָאָמַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל זַבּוֹנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how step 17 reads רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל means a complete sale
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A partial sale is also possible, and that would match the ברייתא's סידור instead of contradicting it.

steps.title: Rejected: for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, nothing is unfit for a Jew
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the partial-sale reading, because according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל no item is ever considered unfit for a Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds this reasoning, that cannot be, because for him there is nothing that is unfit for a person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion from step 18. It says that in רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view, there is no such thing as an item that is 'not fitting' for the debtor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The partial-sale idea depends on sorting items into 'fitting' and 'too fancy.' If every item suits a Jew, nothing can be sold for being too fancy. So רבן שמעון בן גמליאל must mean a full sale. The source for this view comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: If it enters your mind (introduces an idea in order to reject it)

phrases.english: If it enters your mind

phrases.aramaic: אִית לֵיהּ לְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הַאי סְבָרָא,
phrases.english: that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds this reasoning,
there is nothing that is not fitting for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ אִית לֵיהּ לְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הַאי סְבָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the alternative reading offered in step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggestion that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל means only a partial sale
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumes some items are unfit for the debtor, which רבן שמעון בן גמליאל does not accept.

steps.title: אביי: all Jews are children of kings
steps.stepSummary: אביי says that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, רבי שמעון, רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא all hold that every Jew is like a king's child.
steps.simpleTranslation: As אביי said: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, רבי שמעון, רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא all hold: All Jews are children of kings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings אביי's statement as the proof for step 19. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that every Jew is like royalty, so even fancy items suit him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every Jew is a king's child, no item is too fancy for any Jew. So a partial sale of 'unfitting' items can't happen in רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view. His sale must be complete, and רב נחמן's objection stands.

keyTerms.meaning: All Jews are children of kings, so no item is too fine for any Jew

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, collateral is fully sold in court after thirty days. A partial sale is impossible because 'all Jews are children of kings,' so this view leaves no room for סידור. That is why רב נחמן objected to the ברייתא.
steps.whyThisMatters: The idea that 'all Jews are children of kings' appears in several places in ש״ס. Here it shows that a Jew's level of need is never lowered, which affects what can be taken from a debtor.

phrases.english: As Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן,
phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Rabbi Shimon,
and Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabbi Akiva –
all of them hold:
All Jews are children of kings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the rejection in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: That for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, no item is unfit for a Jew
steps.raayaSupportSource: אביי's statement that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, רבי שמעון, רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא hold that all Jews are children of kings

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows moving arum because ravens eat it
steps.stepSummary: The first source for אביי's list: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows moving raw arum on שבת because it is food for ravens.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds this, as we learned in a משנה: One may not move arum or mustard on שבת. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל permits arum, because it is food for ravens.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins proving אביי's statement. It shows where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל treats every Jew like a rich person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Raw arum is not food for people, so the ת"ק treats it as מוקצה. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל permits it because ravens eat it, but only wealthy people keep ravens. Since he permits arum for everyone, he treats every Jew as wealthy.

keyTerms.meaning: Arum, a plant that is not eaten raw

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as we learned:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא אֶת הַלּוּף וְלָא אֶת הַחַרְדָּל.
phrases.english: Not the arum and not the mustard.
phrases.notes: This משנה is in שבת 126b. It is listing raw foods you may not move on שבת.

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל מַתִּיר בַּלּוּף,
phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits arum,
because it is food for ravens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first source for אביי's list of תנאים in step 20.
steps.raayaObject: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that every Jew is like a king's child.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in שבת about moving arum because it is food for ravens.

steps.title: רבי שמעון says all Jews are princes and may use rose oil
steps.stepSummary: The second source: רבי שמעון lets every Jew smear rose oil on wounds on שבת, because all Jews are princes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון holds this, as we learned in a משנה: Princes may smear rose oil on their wounds on שבת, because they usually smear it during the week. רבי שמעון says: All Jews are princes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source, this time for רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Healing on שבת is normally forbidden. Princes may still use rose oil because for them it is ordinary daily use, not medicine. רבי שמעון extends this to every Jew, which shows he holds that all Jews are like kings' children.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon, as we learned:
Princes may smear rose oil
on their wounds on Shabbat,
since it is their way to smear it during the week.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: כׇּל יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּנֵי מְלָכִים הֵן.
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says: All of Israel are princes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of sources, moving from רבן שמעון בן גמליאל to רבי שמעון.
steps.raayaObject: רבי שמעון holds that every Jew is like a king's child.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in שבת about princes using rose oil on שבת.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא say every Jew is fit for the expensive cloak
steps.stepSummary: The third source: the ת"ק says a debtor's very expensive cloak is taken and sold, but רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא say every Jew is worthy of that cloak.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא hold this, as a ברייתא teaches: If someone owed a thousand זוז and was wearing a cloak worth a hundred מנה, the court takes it off him and dresses him in a cloak fit for him. It was taught in the name of רבי ישמעאל, and in the name of רבי עקיבא: All Jews are fit for that cloak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the last source, for רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא. It finishes proving אביי's list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ת"ק holds that a debtor cannot keep a luxury cloak, so the court swaps it for a plainer one and uses it to pay the debt. רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא disagree: since every Jew is worthy of the finest cloak, it counts as his normal clothing and is not taken.

keyTerms.meaning: A coin worth one hundred זוז

steps.whatToRemember: Four תנאים, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, רבי שמעון, רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא, all treat every Jew as worthy of the finest things: arum for ravens, rose oil, and a costly cloak.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, as it is taught:

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיוּ נוֹשִׁין בּוֹ אֶלֶף זוּז
phrases.english: If they were claiming from him a thousand zuz
and he was wearing a cloak worth a hundred maneh,
phrases.notes: A hundred מנה is ten thousand זוז, ten times what he owes.

phrases.english: they strip it from him
and dress him in a cloak fit for him.
And it was taught in the name of Rabbi Yishmael,
and it was taught in the name of Rabbi Akiva:
All of Israel are fit for that cloak.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the list of sources for אביי's statement.
steps.raayaObject: רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא hold that every Jew is like a king's child.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא about a debtor wearing a very expensive cloak.

steps.title: How could a plow be partly sold?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the partial-sale idea from step 18. It works for bedding, but it is hard to see how it works for a plow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to what we first thought, that he gives him what is fit for him and we sell what is not fit for him: That works for a pillow and cushion, because the difference between expensive and plain ones can be sold. But a plow, what is it fit for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the idea it already rejected in step 19. It asks a further question showing that the idea was hard even on its own terms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the partial-sale idea, the court sells a costly item, gives the debtor a cheaper one that suits him, and keeps the difference. With bedding there can be a luxury version and a plain version. A plow is a work tool, so there seems to be no luxury part to sell.

phrases.english: And according to what entered our minds at first,
phrases.notes: This is the idea from step 18, that only the part he doesn't need is sold.

phrases.english: that he gives him what is fit for him,
and we sell what is not fit for him?
It makes sense for a pillow and cushion,
phrases.notes: Bedding and a plow are the examples in our משנה of things returned to the debtor.

phrases.english: what is fit for him is the in-between.
phrases.notes: He means a plainer middle-level set, so the extra value of the fancy set can be sold.

phrases.english: But a plow, what is it fit for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the sources for אביי, the גמרא goes back to the partial-sale idea from step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The early idea that under רבן שמעון בן גמליאל only the unneeded part of the collateral is sold.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A plow has no luxury part that could be sold while a plainer version is returned, so the משנה's plow example does not fit the idea.

steps.title: The plow is a silver plow
steps.stepSummary: רבא בר רבה answers that the case is a silver plow, which has extra value that can be sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא בר רבה said: A silver plow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא בר רבה answers the question about the plow by explaining that it is made of silver.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A silver plow is worth far more than a working plow. The court could sell it and give the debtor an ordinary plow, so the partial-sale idea works for a plow too.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא בַּר רַבָּה: מַחְרֵישָׁה דְּכַסְפָּא.
phrases.english: Rava bar Rabba said: A silver plow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 24 about the plow.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא): the plow in question is a silver one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A plow is only a work tool, so there is no extra value to sell.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a silver plow, which has extra value that can be sold while an ordinary plow is returned.

steps.title: Why should the lender have to look after the borrower?
steps.stepSummary: רב חגא objects: the lender could simply say, "Your needs are not my problem." אביי begins to respond.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חגא challenges this: Let the lender say to the borrower, "Your needs are not thrown on me!" אביי said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: רב חגא challenges the whole idea of leaving the borrower some of his things, because the lender never agreed to support him. The step ends with אביי starting to answer, so the גמרא is setting up his response in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא only asked how to leave the borrower what he needs, as with bedding and the silver plow. רב חגא now questions why it should be done at all. The lender only lent money, so why should he lose out in order to take care of the borrower?

keyTerms.meaning: He challenges it; a strong objection against what was just said
You are not thrown on me; your needs are not my responsibility

steps.confusionAlert: רב חגא is not asking about bedding or plows in particular. He is attacking the whole idea of leaving the borrower anything at all.

phrases.english: Rav Chagga objects to it:
But let him say to him,
phrases.notes: "He" is the lender, speaking to the borrower.

phrases.english: "You are not thrown upon me!"
phrases.notes: He means: I lent you money. I never took on the job of supporting you.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 25 explained how the silver plow case works, רב חגא steps back and challenges the basic rule of leaving the borrower his necessities.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that some of a borrower's belongings must be left for him when he is paying off a debt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The lender only lent money and took on no duty to support the borrower, so he should be able to collect fully and refuse to worry about the borrower's needs.
